_note: Round-2 checks after the cannabis adjudication (readers 241 to 244), 31 October 2026.

tasks.locator: Long-term effects, 1st paragraph (begins p. 296, continues on p. 297) and 2nd paragraph (p. 297)
tasks.extracted: Second-hand (narrative review): studies of long-term effects rely mainly on retrospective self-report by people who chose to use cannabis; long-term memory impairments have been reported mainly in frequent, heavy use, and confounders (ability before use, alcohol and other drugs, type of cannabis, age at onset, and mental health problems including depression and problem cannabis use) make cause and effect hard to establish. Case-control studies are called inconsistent; the most consistent finding is poorer encoding of new episodic memories, with persisting deficits in some studies over the first few days of abstinence but little evidence of deficits at 28 days (as summarised from a review, ref. 25); working memory, attention and impulsivity findings are mixed; one study found no difference in decision making or risk taking against controls matched for mental-health confounds, although in that study poorer decision-making accuracy went with more symptoms of problem cannabis use (ref. 35).

tasks.locator: Table 1, last column and its footnote (p. 322); Figure 1 (p. 320)
tasks.extracted: Table 1 gives each cohort's approximate change from crude to adjusted odds ratio, computed as (crude OR minus adjusted OR) divided by (crude OR minus 1), without saying which exposure contrast each figure refers to. For NPMS the 80% cannot refer to the ever-use estimate pooled in Figure 1 (adjusted OR 0.72), for which the formula would exceed 100% for any crude OR above 1 (editors' calculation), so the seven percentages may mix ever-use and most-frequent-use contrasts.

tasks.locator: Discussion, concluding paragraph (left column)
tasks.extracted: The authors state, without a calculation or a source, that individual lifetime risk of chronic psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia, even in people who use cannabis regularly, is likely to be low, less than 3%.

tasks.locator: Evidence from Cohort studies › Studies investigating psychotic experiences, 2nd paragraph
tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Gage_2016_EpidemiologicEvidenceReview.pdf (Author's Accepted Manuscript; text extraction, AM p. 17 rendered at 150 dpi)
tasks.extracted: In ALSPAC (ref. 23, a study by the review's first two authors and colleagues), cumulative cannabis use at 16 was associated with psychotic experiences at 18 after adjustment for pre-birth and childhood confounders; after further adjustment for cigarette and other illicit drug use the association attenuated to the null, and its authors discuss the difficulty of separating confounding from mediation and possible over-adjustment with such highly correlated measures.

tasks.locator: Interpretation of the findings › i) Confounding, 1st paragraph (AM pp. 5-6) and 2nd paragraph (AM p. 6)
tasks.extracted: Residual confounding would most likely inflate the estimates: studies adjusting for more confounders showed more attenuation, 60-80% of the unadjusted estimate in the 3 studies that adjusted most comprehensively, and few adjusted for early-life attachment, childhood maltreatment and trauma. Shared genetic effects are judged unlikely to explain the association because schizophrenia risk variants explain little of the variation in cannabis use; a cross-sectional sibling-pair study (association between duration of use and psychotic symptoms within sibling pairs) and fixed-effects regression in Christchurch argue against stable familial confounding; but a co-relative study found the association substantially smaller with closer genetic relatedness, suggesting that population studies overestimate it. No numbers are given for the genetic studies.

tasks.locator: Summary › Interpretation
tasks.extracted: The authors read the evidence as consistent with the view that cannabis increases the risk of psychotic outcomes independently of confounding and transient intoxication, judge that further longitudinal studies are unlikely to resolve whether cannabis causes psychosis, and conclude that there is now sufficient evidence to warn young people that using cannabis could increase their risk of a psychotic illness later in life.

tasks.locator: Figure 1 (p. 320); Results, 6th to 9th paragraphs and Figure 2 (p. 321); Table 1, last column and its footnote (p. 322)
tasks.extracted: Pooled adjusted odds ratios: any psychotic outcome after ever use 1.41 (1.20 to 1.65), seven cohorts; most frequent use against none 2.09 (1.54 to 2.84), six cohorts; psychotic disorder after ever use 2.58 (1.08 to 6.13), three cohorts. Table 1 gives each cohort's approximate change from crude to adjusted odds ratio, (crude OR minus adjusted OR) divided by (crude OR minus 1), without saying which exposure contrast it refers to; for NPMS the 80% cannot refer to the ever-use estimate of Figure 1 (adjusted OR 0.72), for which the formula would exceed 100% (editors' calculation).

tasks.locator: Evidence inconsistent with a causal relationship, single paragraph (AM p. 11); References 58 to 61 (AM p. 17)
tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Gage_2016_EpidemiologicEvidenceReview.pdf (Author's Accepted Manuscript; text extraction, AM p. 17 rendered at 150 dpi)
tasks.extracted: Among studies finding no change or a decrease in the incidence of psychotic outcomes the review cites ref. 61, Frisher et al. (2009, Schizophrenia Research), on the impact of cannabis use on trends in diagnosed schizophrenia in the United Kingdom from 1996 to 2005, a published paper; among studies finding increases, ref. 59, Boydell et al. (2003), on the incidence of schizophrenia in south-east London between 1965 and 1997 (refs 58 and 60 do not concern trends by their titles). The review gives as reasons for calling such evidence weak the ecological fallacy, unaccounted confounders and other risk factors that may have declined; it does not discuss diagnostic or service changes.

tasks.locator: Discussion, paragraph on projected trends (p. 326); References 60 and 61 (p. 328)
tasks.extracted: The review cites, without analysing them, two projections of schizophrenia trends: ref. 60, Degenhardt, Hall and Lynskey (2003), and ref. 61, Hickman et al. (2007), model projections for England and Wales. By authors, year and title these are the Australian and British modelling studies that Hall and Degenhardt (2009, refs 88 and 89) and Hall (2015, refs 98 and 99) cite (editors' cross-check of the reference lists).

tasks.locator: Literature Review › 8. Experiment, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Only the rise in UK cannabis use, at least tenfold since the 1970s, is attributed to Gage et al. (ref. 2); the statement that data on first admissions for schizophrenia show no increase, and perhaps a slight decrease, over that time carries no citation.

tasks.locator: Assessment of Tobacco Use and Dependence, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Analysis Procedures, 1st paragraph
tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Anthony_1994_ComparativeEpidemiologyDependence.pdf (scanned copy with an OCR text layer; checked on the page rendered at 150 dpi)
tasks.extracted: Tobacco was handled differently from the other drugs: DSM-III-R tobacco dependence was assessed only in a representative subsample of 4,414 participants (55% of the sample), with questions about daily smoking only, and tobacco use was taken from special analyses of the 1991 National Household Survey on Drug Abuse restricted to ages 15 to 54; the share of people who smoked who became dependent was therefore obtained by division, and no standard errors were estimated for tobacco (also card sc_anthony_1994, key finding 4).

tasks.locator: Abstract › Results
tasks.extracted: Second-hand: around one in 10 people who use cannabis regularly develop dependence; the body, the conclusions and Table 1 give the figure for everyone who has ever used, so the abstract changes the denominator (card reporting issue 1).

tasks.locator: Addiction Considerations, 1st paragraph (p. e13); Reference 58 (p. e21)
tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Page_2020_AHAStatement.pdf (online-first version, pages e1-e22; p. e13 checked on the page rendered at 150 dpi)
tasks.extracted: Second-hand: using data from the US national survey NESARC, Hasin et al. (ref 58, by its title a 2016 analysis of DSM-5 cannabis use disorder in the 2012 to 2013 survey) reported that 3 of 10 people who had used cannabis in the past year met criteria for a use disorder; the statement adds that the prevalence may be higher because the estimates rest on self-report and may use the older DSM-IV criteria. The same paragraph says addiction has been reported in about 9% of people who use cannabis, 17% of those who start in adolescence and 25% to 50% of those who use daily, with no citation on that sentence.

tasks.locator: Cannabis addiction and withdrawal, 2nd paragraph (p. 299); References 71 to 73 and 77 (p. 304)
tasks.extracted: Second-hand: a withdrawal syndrome said to affect around 50% of people who use daily when they stop, typically beginning 1-2 days after stopping, peaking at 2-6 days and fading by 1-2 weeks (ref 71, a 2004 review by Budney and colleagues); prominent symptoms craving, sleep problems, nightmares, anger, irritability, dysphoria and nausea (ref 72, Allsop and colleagues, 2011); symptoms can be alleviated by THC in a dose-dependent way (ref 73, by its title a study of oral THC suppressing cannabis withdrawal symptoms, Budney et al., 2007); in people who use cannabis and tobacco daily, combined withdrawal is stronger than withdrawal from either alone (ref 77).

tasks.locator: Cannabis addiction › Possible treatments for cannabis addiction, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: CB1 receptor agonists, dronabinol (oral synthetic THC) and nabiximols (described as an oral spray with THC and CBD in equal ratio), attenuated cannabis withdrawal symptoms and improved retention in treatment but did not reduce cannabis use compared with placebo.

tasks.page: pp. e13, e20 of the online-first PDF
tasks.locator: Chronic Side Effects, 1st paragraph (p. e13); References 5 and 12 (p. e20)
tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Page_2020_AHAStatement.pdf (online-first version, pages e1-e22; p. e13 checked on the page rendered at 150 dpi)
tasks.extracted: Second-hand: people who use long term may have a withdrawal syndrome when cannabis is suddenly stopped, the dose is decreased or the formulation is changed; signs include anger, anxiety, restlessness, irritability, depressed mood, disturbed sleep, strange dreams, decreased appetite, weight loss, headache and night sweats; symptoms typically begin a few days after stopping or reducing use, peak after about 10 days and end after 30 days (refs 5 and 12, a Health Canada information document for health care professionals and a report of the US National Academies).

tasks.page: pp. e17–e18 of the online-first PDF
tasks.locator: Patient Education and Considerations, 1st paragraph (begins on p. e17; the withdrawal sentences are on p. e18)
tasks.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Page_2020_AHAStatement.pdf (online-first version, pages e1-e22; pp. e17-e18 checked on the pages rendered at 110 and 150 dpi)
tasks.extracted: Recommendation, with no citation on these sentences: people who use cannabis heavily over the long term should be advised not to stop suddenly because of the risk of cannabis withdrawal syndrome, and should contact their provider at once if signs of withdrawal or of hyperemesis syndrome arise.

tasks.locator: Reproductive effects of cannabis use › Fetal development and birth defects, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (begins p. 3, continues p. 4)
tasks.extracted: As summarized: birth defects were not consistently increased, the most convincing null result coming from a large study that measured use by urinalysis; a meta-analysis of studies from the 1980s and 1990s found that regular use in pregnancy reduced birth weight, less than tobacco smoking did; several later large studies found reduced birth weight, an effect that has generally persisted after statistical control for other drug use, and some reported shorter labour and more babies small for gestational age. Limitations named: self-reported use is low and, by urinalysis studies, under-reported, which probably weakens the associations; and it has often been difficult to adjust fully for cigarette smoking.

tasks.page: pp. e10, e12, e14, e17, e21 of the online-first PDF
tasks.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 5th paragraph (p. e10); Table 3, row Hemachandra et al (p. e12); Considerations in Special Populations › Young Adults, paragraph (p. e14); Patients With Cardiac Risk Factors, paragraph (p. e17); References, ref 68 (p. e21)
tasks.extracted: As relayed: in a population survey (PATH Through Life, age cohorts 20–24, 40–44 and 60–64, surveyed 1999–2002; Hemachandra et al.), people with past-year cannabis use (n = 1043) had 3.3 times the rate of stroke or transient ischaemic attack (95% CI 1.8 to 6.3), a rate ratio of 2.3 (1.1 to 4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related covariates including tobacco smoking, with stroke or TIA in people using weekly or more often (4.7, 2.1 to 10.7) and no elevation at lower frequency. In the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, among adults aged 18 to 44 (Parekh et al., 2020, ref 68), the adjusted OR for stroke was 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10) for people who used marijuana against those who did not, 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) for use on more than 10 days a month, 3.12 (1.40 to 6.97) for frequent use with combustible cigarettes and 2.63 (1.07 to 6.46) with e-cigarettes; adjustment sets not stated. The text and Table 3 give different cohort sizes (study card reporting issue).

tasks.page: pp. e11, e17, e21–e22 of the online-first PDF
tasks.locator: Table 3, row DeFilippis et al (p. e11); Considerations in Special Populations › Comorbid Cardiovascular Disease, paragraph (p. e17); References, refs 32, 37 and 87 (pp. e21–e22)
tasks.extracted: As relayed: in 2097 young adults with myocardial infarction at 2 academic hospitals, 2000–2016 (DeFilippis et al., 2018, ref 32, titled as a study of cocaine and marijuana use), adjusted HRs of 1.99 for all-cause and 2.22 for cardiovascular mortality are given among people who used cocaine and marijuana (no intervals; whether the exposures were combined is not said); the text says cannabis use is present in 6% of patients aged 50 or younger presenting with AMI and is associated with worse all-cause and cardiovascular mortality. The text adds that smaller studies (refs 37 and 87: Frost et al., 2013, on long-term mortality among survivors of myocardial infarction, and Mukamal et al., 2008, an exploratory prospective study of mortality after myocardial infarction, by their titles) have shown a signal toward higher mortality in coronary artery disease with cannabis use, although many of these findings failed to reach statistical significance.
